title: US Green Card Freeze at Eight Tech Firms: What H-1B Workers Actually Face
excerpt: The Department of Labor has barred Microsoft, Adobe, TCS, Infosys and four others from PERM labour certification. Your H-1B is safe — but the road to a green card just got longer for thousands of Indian tech workers.
body:
• The US Department of Labor has suspended eight companies — Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, TCS, Wipro, HCLTech and Capgemini — from the PERM labour-certification programme, freezing new and pending green-card filings linked to them.
  • Your H-1B visa is NOT affected: PERM and H-1B are separate programmes. The freeze does not revoke existing visas or green cards — it blocks one route to permanent residency.
  • If your employer is on the list: talk to your immigration attorney this week about pending PERM filings, know your I-140 priority date status, and keep your H-1B extensions on schedule — the suspension touches labour certification only.
  • The administration links the move to federal investigations into H-1B and green-card abuse; India's foreign ministry called the freeze harmful to shared ambitions and Vance's "indentured servants" remark "deeply offensive."

The Trump administration has suspended eight major technology and IT services companies from the US Permanent Labour Certification (PERM) programme, throwing the green-card pipeline of thousands of Indian tech workers into uncertainty. The order, announced on October 8 by Labor Secretary Keith Sonderling alongside Vice President JD Vance, bars the eight companies from submitting new PERM applications and halts processing of pending ones.

The eight companies named are Microsoft, Adobe, Cognizant, Infosys, Tata Consultancy Services (TCS), Wipro, HCL Technologies and Capgemini. According to officials, the Department of Labor cited multiple ongoing federal investigations and accused the companies of abusing the labour-certification system to replace American workers with lower-paid foreign employees.

PERM is not H-1B — and that distinction matters

The single most important thing for workers to understand is the mechanism. H-1B is a temporary work visa that lets employers hire foreign professionals for a fixed period. PERM is a separate, employer-led process in which a company certifies to the Labor Department that no qualified American worker was available for a position — a mandatory first step before sponsoring most EB-2 and EB-3 employment-based green cards.

https://x.com/timesofindia/status/2108766175648010357

The suspension applies to PERM applications. As India's Ministry of External Affairs stated: "The suspension of PERM applications does not, by itself, affect the validity of existing H-1B visas or the status of H-1B visa holders and their dependents." Existing green cards are untouched. What freezes is the path from a temporary work visa to permanent residency for employees whose cases depend on PERM sponsorship from one of the eight firms.

"The steps announced by the US do not advance the shared ambitions of both countries."

— India's Ministry of External Affairs

Who feels it first

The immediate pain falls on workers whose PERM cases were pending or about to be filed at one of the eight companies. Mint's explainer notes that these workers face delays and greater uncertainty about permanent residency, even as they can keep working on their H-1Bs. For the companies, the measure complicates talent retention — the promise of green-card sponsorship is one of the strongest incentives for skilled workers to stay put.

The eight firms employ enormous numbers of Indian professionals. Microsoft has said that roughly 80% of its approximately 6,000 H-1B applications last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of existing employees, and that the vast majority of its US employees are Americans — a defence against the administration's claim that the programmes displace American workers.

Some routes remain open. Mint notes that certain EB-2 National Interest Waiver cases and other categories that do not depend on PERM may be exempt from the freeze, though workers should confirm with counsel rather than assume.

The political backdrop

The freeze is part of a broader offensive against the skilled-immigration system. Vance has characterised H-1B workers as "foreign indentured servants" — language India's foreign ministry called "unwarranted and deeply offensive." The administration has also extended the $100,000 H-1B fee into September 2027 and tied new filings to employer layoff history.

The Indian response has been unusually sharp. Alongside the MEA's statement, Zoho founder Sridhar Vembu urged Indian tech professionals in the US to return and help build India's technology sector — an appeal backed by Union Minister Dharmendra Pradhan. The message from Delhi is two-sided: talent mobility benefits both economies, but India is positioning itself as the fallback.

What to watch

The suspension is tied to the outcome of federal investigations, which means there is no fixed end date. Watch for three things: whether the Labor Department names additional companies, whether courts entertain challenges from affected employers, and whether the administration's immigration posture hardens further in the December rule-making season. For workers, the practical watch-list is simpler: your attorney, your priority date, and your employer's compliance status.
